facts.query: What are the biggest milestones in the history of medicine?
facts.explanation: Medicine moved from careful observation in ancient Greece to anatomy, microscopes and vaccines, then to anaesthesia, X-rays and antibiotics. The twentieth century added insulin, the structure of DNA, organ transplants and the eradication of smallpox.

facts.label: Hippocrates
facts.description: Around this time the Greek physician Hippocrates and his followers treat disease as natural rather than supernatural.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica; date approximate (Hippocrates lived c. 460–370 BCE)

facts.label: Vesalius's anatomy
facts.description: Andreas Vesalius publishes De humani corporis fabrica, the first modern atlas of human anatomy.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica

facts.label: Blood circulation
facts.description: William Harvey shows that the heart pumps blood around the body in a closed circuit.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica

facts.label: Microbes seen
facts.description: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek reports tiny living 'animalcules' seen through his microscopes.
facts.sourceNote: Royal Society, Philosophical Transactions archive

facts.label: First vaccine
facts.description: Edward Jenner uses cowpox to protect a boy against smallpox, the first vaccine.
facts.sourceNote: WHO history of smallpox vaccination

facts.label: Stethoscope
facts.description: René Laennec invents the stethoscope.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica

facts.label: Ether anaesthesia
facts.description: First public demonstration of surgery under ether anaesthesia in Boston.
facts.sourceNote: Massachusetts General Hospital history

facts.label: X-rays
facts.description: Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays.
facts.sourceNote: Nobel Prize in Physics 1901 records

facts.label: Blood groups
facts.description: Karl Landsteiner discovers the ABO blood groups, making safe transfusions possible.
facts.sourceNote: Nobel Prize in Medicine 1930 records

facts.label: Insulin
facts.description: Insulin is first used to treat a person with diabetes.
facts.sourceNote: Nobel Prize in Medicine 1923 records

facts.label: Penicillin
facts.description: Alexander Fleming discovers penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic.
facts.sourceNote: Nobel Prize in Medicine 1945 records

facts.label: DNA structure
facts.description: Watson and Crick, using Rosalind Franklin's data, describe the double helix of DNA.
facts.sourceNote: Nature, 25 April 1953

facts.label: Heart transplant
facts.description: Christiaan Barnard performs the first human heart transplant in Cape Town.
facts.sourceNote: Groote Schuur Hospital records

facts.label: Smallpox eradicated
facts.description: The World Health Assembly declares smallpox eradicated.
facts.sourceNote: WHO

facts.label: Human genome
facts.description: The Human Genome Project completes its sequence of human DNA.
facts.sourceNote: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

facts.query: If the history of life on Earth were squeezed into one day, when would humans appear?
facts.topic: History of life in a day
facts.explanation: Squeeze Earth's whole history into one day and life appears early, but complex cells take most of the day to arrive. Animals show up in the evening, dinosaurs vanish shortly before midnight, and our own species appears only in the final seconds.

facts.label: Earth forms
facts.description: The Earth forms from the disc of material around the young Sun.
facts.sourceNote: US Geological Survey (radiometric dating: 4.54 billion years)

facts.label: First life
facts.description: Earliest evidence of microbial life; the exact date is still debated.
facts.sourceNote: Peer-reviewed fossil and isotope studies (estimates 3.5–3.8 billion years ago)

facts.label: Oxygen builds up
facts.description: The Great Oxidation Event: oxygen from microbes starts to build up in the air.
facts.sourceNote: Geological studies of the Great Oxidation Event (about 2.4 billion years ago)

facts.label: Complex cells
facts.description: First eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, the kind that make up our bodies.
facts.sourceNote: Fossil record estimates (about 1.6–2.1 billion years ago)

facts.label: First animals
facts.description: Simple multicellular animals appear in the oceans.
facts.sourceNote: Fossil and molecular estimates (about 600 million years ago)

facts.label: Cambrian explosion
facts.description: Most major animal groups appear in a burst of evolution.
facts.sourceNote: International Commission on Stratigraphy (start of the Cambrian, 538.8 million years ago)

facts.label: Fish walk on land
facts.description: Fish-like animals such as Tiktaalik begin moving onto land.
facts.sourceNote: Daeschler, Shubin and Jenkins (2006), Nature

facts.label: First mammals
facts.description: Small early mammals live alongside the dinosaurs.
facts.sourceNote: Fossil record estimates (about 200 million years ago)

facts.label: Dinosaurs die out
facts.description: An asteroid impact ends the age of dinosaurs.
facts.sourceNote: International Commission on Stratigraphy (end of the Cretaceous)

facts.label: Human lineage splits
facts.description: Our ancestors split from the line leading to chimpanzees.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Human Origins Program (about 6–7 million years ago)

facts.label: Homo sapiens
facts.description: The oldest known fossils of our species, from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco.
facts.sourceNote: Hublin et al. (2017), Nature

facts.label: Farming begins
facts.description: People begin farming in the Fertile Crescent.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Human Origins Program (about 12,000 years ago)

plan.title: The history of life in one day
plan.caption: Now is midnight. Our species arrives in the last few seconds.

facts.query: How does blood flow through the heart?
facts.explanation: The heart is two pumps side by side. The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, and the left side sends oxygen-rich blood out to the rest of the body, in a loop that never stops.

facts.label: Blood returns
facts.title: Blood returns to the heart
facts.description: Oxygen-poor blood from the body flows through the large veins into the right atrium.
facts.sourceNote: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute: How the Heart Works

facts.label: Right ventricle
facts.title: Right ventricle pumps
facts.description: The blood passes into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the pulmonary artery.
facts.sourceNote: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute: How the Heart Works

facts.label: Lungs
facts.title: Blood picks up oxygen
facts.description: In the lungs the blood releases carbon dioxide and picks up fresh oxygen.
facts.sourceNote: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute: How the Heart Works

facts.label: Left atrium
facts.title: Back to the heart
facts.description: Oxygen-rich blood returns through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.
facts.sourceNote: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute: How the Heart Works

facts.label: Left ventricle
facts.title: Left ventricle pumps
facts.description: The strong left ventricle pumps the blood into the aorta, the body's largest artery.
facts.sourceNote: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute: How the Heart Works

facts.label: Body
facts.title: Oxygen delivered
facts.description: Arteries and tiny capillaries deliver oxygen to every tissue, then veins carry the blood back.
facts.sourceNote: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute: How the Heart Works

facts.query: How many heartbeats does it take to pump all your blood?
facts.explanation: Each beat of the left ventricle pushes out a small cupful of blood. Add enough beats together and the heart moves the body's entire blood supply, which at rest takes roughly a minute.

facts.label: Blood pumped per heartbeat at rest (typical adult)
facts.sourceNote: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology: resting stroke volume about 70 mL

facts.label: Total blood in an adult body
facts.sourceNote: NIH MedlinePlus and physiology textbooks: about 5 litres in an average adult
